# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, money and sending, but the 'Offer a pilot?' screen sits after the commitment step it depends on and is separated from it by the check screen, when it belongs right beside 'first real step' in the money section.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same question, and screens 14, 15 and 16 all come back to who decides and pays after screen 10 already asked it; as a founder whose wearer decides alone, I answered the same thing again at 14.
founder.missing: Nothing asks what the product depends on before it can work (a phone with Bluetooth and internet, English-speaking conversation partners), nothing asks about HSA/FSA eligibility, which changes who really pays and how the price feels, and the price screen has no way to enter a one-off hardware purchase plus an optional subscription ($599 glasses, $20/month Pro), so I had to force it onto a yearly figure.

PRIMARY.missing: Whether the captions keep up and stay accurate in noisy places like a theatre lobby or a restaurant, how they work with my hearing aids or glasses, and what I use now to follow conversations.

screens.instead: Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults who talk with hearing people every week would order a pair of caption glasses at $599 with free returns now. Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out and right after I set the commitment step, it makes sense to ask whether people who answer can raise their hand for a pilot.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is plain to a startup founder, but for glasses I sell with free returns I would have to think about what a pilot means here, since the screen does not say what the person would get or do.
screens.why3: Whether I would run a pilot with early wearers is my own decision and I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: The only visible control is Continue, which works as an implicit skip, but there is no explicit yes or no and no sign of how to offer a pilot or what I would be committing to.
screens.why5: It adds nothing to or changes nothing in what I typed, and it says plainly that my respondents' answers are unaffected.
screens.instead: Do you want people who finish the study to be able to ask to try the glasses early? Options: Yes, let them ask / No, not this time.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, it makes sense to settle how strangers will get the questions, especially since my people are deaf or hard of hearing and may not be able to use a spoken interview.
screens.why2: "Who should ask them" is clear, but "this account runs on its own AI" and "Keel's credits" take a second read, and they don't say plainly whether I have a real choice right now.
screens.why3: I know how my deaf and hard-of-hearing users take in questions, so I can answer this from daily experience with them.
screens.why4: A locked, preselected face isn't much of a choice, and nothing says the AI interviewer is captioned or that reading and tapping is the right fit for deaf people, which is the option I would actually pick.
screens.why5: The screen doesn't restate or change anything I typed about AirCaps, the wearer or the job, so my meaning is intact.
screens.instead: How should people get your questions? Options: They read and tap their answers (no sound needed, included with your account) / An AI interviewer talks with them, with captions on screen (uses Keel credits).

screens.why1: Once I've decided to send the study, it's obvious I need to choose the format strangers will answer in, and this matters a lot for deaf and hard-of-hearing people.
screens.why2: I get the choice, but the question says "answer" while the options are mostly about how the question is asked, and "Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud" takes a second read to see it means how much of what people say gets heard correctly.
screens.why3: I know how my people communicate, so I can see at once that text is the safe route and that a spoken interview shuts some of them out.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and my true answer, Text only, is there, but the AI interviewer's pitch is all about noise and never says whether the questions are captioned, which is what a deaf respondent needs to know.
screens.why5: My "Text only" is kept, but the screen is generic: it pitches questions asked aloud to a study of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults with no sign that it took in who I said they are.
screens.instead: How should they answer? Text only: they read each question and tap or type (best for people who can't hear a spoken question). AI interviewer: a face on video asks aloud with captions on screen, and they can talk, type or tap (needs Keel's credits). Let them choose: they pick when they open the link (needs Keel's credits).

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how people answer, the obvious last step is deciding who gets the link, though the 'Sent' kicker reads oddly when nothing has gone out yet.
screens.why2: The question and the first and third options are plain on first reading, but 'the Contacts page' and 'pick a list' refer to something no earlier screen has shown me, so I'd need a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I can reach: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know by name and the community groups where others already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, and my answer of named people is there, so no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: My pick of people by name is kept as I'd say it, and nothing on the screen changes what I typed about AirCaps or the people I'm studying.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I know by name (each gets their own link) / People I find with a Keel search (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group where one open link gets posted (each person signs in with Google).

screens.why1: It is the first screen and it says it is an idea to consider, so it makes sense to be shown the idea before being asked anything about it.
screens.why2: Glasses, live captions and eye contact are everyday words for me, and I understood it on first reading, though "an app on them" is slightly odd for glasses.
screens.why3: Captions and trying to read someone while keeping eye contact are my daily life, so I can picture wearing these in a real conversation.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read, with no options, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The product name is shown on purpose and the idea is clear, but "the wearer" is a maker's term and the belief line only repeats the sentence before it, so it tells me nothing about what they actually believe.
screens.why6: The short sentences say well, but "read the words while keeping eye contact" is heard twice in a row, and the last sentence sounds like a repeat rather than something new to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps. You wear lightweight glasses that show live captions of what people nearby are saying, inside the lens. The people building it believe you could follow a conversation while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: It makes sense to ask how often this happens to me, but it comes straight after the idea card with nothing to say which kind of conversation it means.
screens.why2: I know the word 'miss', but I'd have to stop and work out whether it means conversations I stayed away from or ones I sat through and couldn't follow.
screens.why3: Losing conversations is my everyday life, but nobody keeps count over a month, especially when it's bits of a chat rather than whole ones, so any number would be a guess.
screens.why4: The number box and 'I don't know' fit, but 'Nothing' is an odd answer to 'how many' when I'd say 'None', and 'I'd rather not say' is one escape too many.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'miss' has drifted from not being able to follow or join a face-to-face conversation, and 'face to face' has gone altogether.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is short, one question with one escape, and I could take it in once and answer with a number.
screens.instead: Think of the last 7 days: about how many face-to-face conversations with hearing people did you lose track of or drop out of? Type a number, or choose None or I can't recall.

screens.why1: Asking what it's worth makes sense once I've seen the idea, but it comes straight after how many conversations I missed, under a heading that says "What you do today", so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: "Worth to you up front" and "a month" are plain, and I'd understand them on first reading, the way I'd think about paying for hearing aids and then a subscription.
screens.why3: I know what hearing aids and captioning cost me and what missing conversations costs me, but I've never bought this, so my figure would be partly a guess.
screens.why4: The bands share their edges, so $599, $1,000 and $2,500 each fit two options and $20 and $50 do the same on the monthly list, though the true answer is there and "I can't say" fits.
screens.why5: The name on the card is shown on purpose, but a band edge as exact as $599 among round numbers makes me suspect that's the price they already have in mind, which nudges my answer.
screens.why6: Two price questions run together with twelve dollar ranges to hold, six rungs read at once instead of being split up, and the escape is said only once and comes out as the clumsy "Or say I can't say".
screens.instead: What's the most you would pay up front for AirCaps? Under $250; $250 to $599; $600 to $1,000; $1,001 to $2,500; or over $2,500. Or say I can't say. (Asked in two steps aloud, with "I wouldn't pay for this" taken first and the monthly question asked separately, in non-overlapping bands: under $10; $10 to $19; $20 to $49; $50 to $99; or $100 or more.)

screens.why1: I just gave a price, so asking what would make it worth more follows straight on and I can see why it is here.
screens.why2: Short everyday words, and I understand it the first time I read it or have it captioned.
screens.why3: I can say what I would need in a noisy restaurant or at the theatre, but I have only seen a card about AirCaps and never worn them, so part of my answer is a guess.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the product name I was already shown, but "$250 to $599 once" reads like a catalogue line, and I would say "You said $250 to $599, paid once."
screens.why6: It is one short question that is easy to follow, but "$250 to $599 once" is a mouthful when said aloud and the "once" hangs oddly at the end.
screens.instead: You said you'd pay $250 to $599 for AirCaps, paid one time. What would make them worth more to you?

screens.why1: I just put AirCaps at up to $599, so asking next whether I could actually pay that makes obvious sense, even though the 'What you do today' label doesn't quite match.
screens.why2: I understand the $599, but 'money you already spend' doesn't say spend on what, and I had to stop and work out what 'this' covers.
screens.why3: I know what I can afford, but I don't have a regular budget for anything like this, so I'd be guessing which pot of money it would really come from.
screens.why4: 'From money I already spend on this' is odd when I've never bought anything like this, and there's no option for insurance or a vocational rehab agency helping, though 'I can't say' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The $599 is the top of the range I was just shown, and nothing beyond the idea I've already seen leaks through or sounds like company talk.
screens.why6: It's short and I could hold the three options, but 'or not?' sets up a yes or no that the options don't answer, and 'Or say I can't say' sounds clumsy.
screens.instead: Could you pay about $599 once for AirCaps, or not? Yes, from what I spend on hearing help; Yes, from savings; Yes, if insurance or an agency helped; No, I couldn't pay it; or say I can't say.

screens.why1: After asking whether I could pay $599, it makes sense to ask who else has a say, but it sounds like a work purchase and feels a bit abrupt for something I'd buy for my own ears.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but 'something like this' makes me stop and wonder whether it means caption glasses, a captioning app or my hearing aids.
screens.why3: I've never bought caption glasses, so I'd have to guess which past purchase counts, though I do know who had a say when I bought my hearing aids.
screens.why4: 'No, someone else decided for me' is an odd answer to 'did anyone else have to agree', the two 'Yes' options overlap, and nothing fits if I've never paid for anything like this except a loose 'I can't recall one'.
screens.why5: No company roles or product terms reach me here, and the question still simply asks who had to agree to the purchase.
screens.why6: It is one short question and a sayable list, but the options jump between yes, no, yes and no, so they are hard to hold after one hearing.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing or captioning product, who made the decision? I decided alone; I decided with one other person; I decided with several people; or someone else decided for me. Or say I can't recall one.

screens.why1: After the price and paying questions, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last step.
screens.why2: Ordering a pair with free returns is plain to me, though the card's bare 'Imagine AirCaps' only makes sense because I saw the idea earlier.
screens.why3: I can answer this from my own life, because I know whether I'd risk ordering something that might help me follow people at the theatre or at a noisy table.
screens.why4: The three options cover my answer, but 'Probably not' has no matching 'Probably yes', so a hopeful-but-unsure person like me is pushed towards one side, and the first option repeats the whole question.
screens.why5: An idea card shown on purpose names AirCaps, and nothing here leaks a plan or any words about people that I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It is short and says easily as one question, but repeating 'order a pair with free returns' in the first option is a mouthful just after hearing it in the stem.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order a pair; Maybe, I'd want to know more; or No.
